name: project-git
description: How git works in an Archon Horizon workspace — one out-of-tree workspace ledger (no per-project repos); read a project's history by pathspec or by a session's commit trailers.
---

Read this before running `git diff`/`git log` on a project.

## The model

- **One out-of-tree workspace ledger.** Archon commits to a single repo whose git
  dir is `.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git` with the workspace **root** as its
  work tree (driven via `--git-dir`/`--work-tree`). `<root>/.git` is deliberately
  untouched — it is reserved for a user repo. The ledger records one commit per
  completed session: `config.yaml`, the session's scoped project files, and
  `.archon-horizon/` shared state; never the binary git dirs under
  `.archon-horizon/vcs/`, locks, or other volatile internals.
- **There are no per-project repositories.** A project directory has no nested
  `.git/`, and there is no `.archon-horizon/vcs/<project>.git`. A project's
  "history" is simply the workspace ledger filtered to that project's path.
- **You record your own work by committing to the ledger** with plain `git` (see
  below). Commit after each independently useful, verified proof/file/tooling
  change, before a long build or delegated review, and before expanding scope.
  A multi-hour implementation session should normally have several commits; one
  commit is appropriate only when the work is genuinely atomic. The message +
  diff is how progress is read, so use a semantic, math-first subject. Provenance
  trailers are added automatically; do not write them.

So a plain `git diff` at the root sees only a user repo (if any), never Archon's.
Drive the out-of-tree workspace ledger explicitly (or use `hgit`).

## Recording your work (committing)

Commits go to the ledger, **not** to `<root>/.git` and **not** via any project
`.git` (there is none). Do **not** `export GIT_DIR` / `GIT_WORK_TREE` yourself — that
would redirect `lake` and other tooling. Two equivalent ways to commit:

```bash
# 1) The `hgit` wrapper (on the session env as $HORIZON_GIT) — plain git, ledger-scoped:
"$HORIZON_GIT" add path/to/File.lean
"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
  --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'

# 2) The explicit form (identical effect):
git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
    add path/to/File.lean
git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
    commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
    --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'
```

Ordinary git: the ledger's index tracks HEAD, so `add` then `commit` records your
files on top of it. Horizon's own commits stage in a private index and never leave
anything staged in your way.

- **Prefer the pathspec commit** — name the paths on the commit itself:
  `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "…" --trailer 'Summary=…' -- path/to/File.lean`
  It records exactly those files, ignores whatever else may be staged, and git
  builds its tree from the **current** HEAD — so it cannot silently revert a
  concurrent session's files the way a commit built on a stale index can.
- Add at least one **`Summary` trailer** explaining the important change, not
  merely repeating the subject. Use one trailer per distinct explanation when
  useful. Its value supports Markdown and LaTeX, so concise mathematical context
  such as `--trailer 'Summary=**Invariant.** Preserves $f(x)=x$ on $A$.'` renders
  directly in the dashboard commit item. Keep each trailer on one line; repeat
  `--trailer 'Summary=…'` for a few separate points.
- Do not wait for the whole task to be complete. A checkpoint commit must build
  or otherwise be internally coherent, but it may explicitly leave the next
  named obligation open.
- Stage **explicit paths** you changed rather than `add -A` — the work tree is the
  whole workspace, so `-A` can sweep in unrelated files.
- `Archon-Run`/`Session`/`Role`/`Task`/`Projects` trailers are stamped for you by a
  hook from the session env; your message stays clean.
- Build artifacts (`.lake`, `*.olean`, …) are excluded automatically, and any
  high-confidence credential is **redacted to `XXXX`** in the staged content (not
  blocked), so a broad add still won't leak a secret into the ledger.
- If the guard reports *"redacted possible secret(s) to XXXX"*, it scrubbed a
  matched credential and let the commit through — **rotate the real credential**,
  and check you didn't stage more than you meant to (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ALLOW_SECRETS=1`
  skips the scan entirely). A *separate* guard still **blocks** a commit that would
  silently delete tracked files you didn't change (a stale-index clobber); re-seed
  the index (`git read-tree HEAD && git add -- <your files>`) rather than forcing it.

Then verify **in the ledger**, and verify the **paths**, not just the SHA — a bare
`git cat-file` runs against `<root>/.git`, which has not seen your commit yet and will
make a perfectly real SHA look fabricated:

```bash
"$HORIZON_GIT" ls-tree --name-only HEAD -- path/to/File.lean   # empty ⇒ NOT in HEAD
```

## Concurrent sessions and the clobber guard

Several sessions may commit to the ledger at once. A commit whose index was
seeded from an older HEAD (e.g. `read-tree`, then a concurrent session commits,
then you commit) produces a tree that *lacks* the other session's new files —
plain git would commit it without any error and silently delete their work.
The ledger's `pre-commit` guard now rejects any commit that stages deletions
you did not ask for:

1823	\begin{dfn}\label{df:div}
1824	 Define a functor $\Div_{X/S}$ by the formula
1825	    $$\Div_{X/S}(T):=\{\,\text{relative effective divisors $D$
1826	     on $X_T/T$}\,\}.$$
1827	 \end{dfn}

1829	Note $\Div_{X/S}$ is indeed a functor.  Namely, given a relative
1830	effective divisor $D$ on $X_T/T$ and an arbitrary $S$-map $p\:T'\to T$,
1831	we have to see the $T'$-flat closed subscheme $D_{T'}\subset
1832	X_{T'}$ is an effective divisor.  So let $\mc I$ denote the ideal of
1833	$D$.  Since $D$ is $T$-flat, $p_{X_T}^*\mc I$ is equal to the ideal of
1834	$D_{T'}$.  But, since $\mc I$ is invertible, so is $p_{X_T}^*\mc I$.
1835	Thus $D_{T'}$ is a (relative) effective divisor.

1837	\begin{thm}\label{th:repDiv}
1838	 Assume $X/S$ is projective and flat.  Then $\Div_{X/S}$ is
1839	representable by an open subscheme $\IDiv_{X/S}$ of the Hilbert scheme
1840	$\IHilb_{X/S}$.
1841	 \end{thm}
1842	
1843	\begin{proof}
1844	 Set $H:=\IHilb_{X/S}$, and let $W\subset X\x H$ be the universal
1845	(closed) subscheme, and $q\:W\to H$ the projection.  Let $V$ denote the
1846	set of points $w\in W$ at which $W$ is an effective divisor. Plainly $V$
1847	is open in $W$.  Set $Z:=q(W-V)$.  Then $Z$ is closed because $q$ is
1848	proper.  Set $U:=H-Z$.  Then $U$ is open, and $q^{-1}U$ is an effective
1849	divisor in $X\x U$.  In fact, since $q$ is flat, $q^{-1}U$ is a relative
1850	effective divisor in $X\x U/U$.
1851	
1852	It remains to show that $U$ represents $\Div_{X/S}$.  So let $T$ be an
1853	$S$-scheme, and $D\subset X_T/T$ a relative effective divisor.  By the
1854	universal property of the pair $(H,W)$, there exists a unique map
1855	$g\:T\to H$ such that $g_X^{-1}W=D$.  We have to show that $g$ factors
1856	through $U$.
1857	
1858	For each $t\in T$, the fiber $D_t$ is an effective divisor since it is
1859	obtained by base change (or owing to Lemma~\ref{lm:ctn}).  But
1860	$D_t=W_{g(t)}\ox k_t$ where $k_t$ is the residue field of $t$.  So
1861	$W_{g(t)}$ too is a divisor, as a field extension is faithfully flat.
1862	Hence, since $X\x H$ and $W$ are $H$-flat, $W$ is, by
1863	Lemma~\ref{lm:ctn}, a relative effective divisor along the fiber over
1864	$g(t)$.  Therefore, $g(t)\in U$.  So, since $U$ is open, $g$ factors
1865	through $U$.
1866	 \end{proof}

1899	O_{\!X}$-module flat over $S$.  Recall from \cite[7.7.6]{EGAIII2} that there

1906	\cite[7.7.9]{EGAIII2}, forming it commutes with changing the base, in

1910	conditions are equivalent:

1917	F)\ox \mc N\risom f_*(\mc F\ox f^*\mc N)$;

2043	\section{The Picard scheme}\label{sc:Psch}
2044	
2045	This section proves Grothendieck's main theorem about the Picard scheme,
2046	which asserts its existence if $X/S$ is projective and flat and its
2047	geometric fibers are integral; in fact, the functor $\Pic_{(X/S)\et}$ is
2048	representable.  The proof involves Grothendieck's method of using
2049	functors to prescribe patching.  The basic theory is developed in
2050	\cite[Ch.~0, Sct.~4.5, pp.~102--107]{EGAG}, and is applied in
2051	\cite[Ch.~1, Sct.~9, pp.~354--401]{EGAG} to the construction of
2052	Grassmannians and related parameter schemes.  The present construction
2053	involves the basic theory, but is more sophisticated and more
2054	complicated because it works not simply with the Zariski topology, but
2055	also with the \'etale topology.
2056	
2057	\begin{dfn}\label{df:Psch}
2058	 If any of the four relative Picard functors of Definition~\ref{df:Pfs}
2059	is representable, then the representing scheme is called the {\it Picard
2060	scheme\/} and denoted by $\IPic_{X/S}$.  Moreover, we say simply that the
2061	Picard scheme $\IPic_{X/S}$ exists.
2062	 \end{dfn}
2063	
2064	Notice that, although there are four relative Picard functors, there is
2065	at most one Picard scheme.  Of course, if any functor is representable,
2066	then the representing scheme is uniquely determined, up to a unique
2067	isomorphism that preserves the identification of the given functor
2068	with the functor of points of the representing scheme.  But here, there
2069	is more to the story.
2070

2368	\begin{lem}\label{lm:qt}
2369	 Let $\alpha\:Z\to P$ be a map of \'etale sheaves, and set $R:=Z\x_PZ$.
2370	Assume $\alpha$ is a surjection, $Z$ is representable by a
2371	quasi-projective $S$-scheme, $R$ is representable by an $S$-scheme, and
2372	the first projection $R\to Z$ is representable by a smooth and proper
2373	map.  Then $P$ is representable by a quasi-projective $S$-scheme, and
2374	$\alpha$ is representable by a smooth map.
2375	 \end{lem}
2376	
2377	\begin{proof} To lighten the notation, let $Z$ and $R$ denote the
2378	corresponding schemes as well.  Since the structure map $Z\to S$ is
2379	quasi-projective, it is separated; whence, the first projection
2380	$Z\x_SZ\to Z$ is too.  But the first projection $R\to Z$ is proper, and
2381	factors naturally through a map $h\:R\to Z\x_SZ$.  Hence $h$ is proper.
2382	But $h$ is a monomorphism; that is, $h$ is injective on $T$-points.
2383	Therefore, $h$ is a closed embedding by \cite[8.11.5]{EGAIV3}.
2384	
2385	Plainly, for each $S$-scheme $T$, the subset $R(T)\subset
2386	Z(T)\x_{S(T)}Z(T)$ is the graph of an equivalence relation.  Also, the
2387	map of schemes $R\to Z$ is flat and proper, and $Z$ is a
2388	quasi-projective $S$-scheme.  It follows that there exist a
2389	quasi-projective $S$-scheme $Q$ and a faithfully flat and projective map
2390	$Z\to Q$ such that $R=Z\x_QZ$.  (In other words, a flat and proper
2391	equivalence relation on a quasi-projective scheme is effective.)  In
2392	fact, $R$ defines a map from $Z$ to the Hilbert scheme $\IHilb_{Z/S}$, and
2393	its graph lies in the universal scheme as a closed subscheme, which
2394	descends to $Q\subset \IHilb_{Z/S}$; for more details, see \cite[Thm.~(2.9),
2395	p.~70]{AK80}.
2396	
2397	Since $Z\to Q$ is flat, it is smooth if (and only if) its fibers are
2398	smooth.  But these fibers are, up to extension of the ground field, the
2399	same as those of $R\to Z$.  And $R\to Z$ is smooth by hypothesis.  Thus
2400	$Z\to Q$ is smooth.
2401	
2402	It remains to see that $Q$ represents $P$.  First, observe that $Z\to Q$
2403	is (represents) a surjection of \'etale sheaves.  Indeed, given an
2404	element of $Q(T)$, set $A:=Z\x_QT$.  Then $A\to T$ is smooth.  So there
2405	exist an \'etale covering $T'\to T$ and a $T$-map $T'\to A$ by
2406	\cite[17.16.3 (ii)]{EGAIV4}.  Then $T'\to A\to Z$ is an element of
2407	$Z(T')$, which maps to the element of $Q(T')$ induced by the given
2408	element of $Q(T)$.
2409	
2410	Since $Z\to Q$ is a surjection of \'etale sheaves, $Q$ is, in the
2411	category of \'etale sheaves, the coequalizer of the pair of maps
2412	$R\rightrightarrows Z$ by Exercise~\ref{ex:epi} below, which is an
2413	elementary exercise in general Grothendieck topology.  By the same
2414	exercise, $P$ too is the coequalizer of this pair of maps.  But, in any
2415	category, the coequalizer is unique up to unique isomorphism.  Thus $Q$
2416	represents $P$.
2417	 \end{proof}

12	# FGA representability of the Picard scheme
13	
14	This file states the FGA representability of the relative Picard functor of a
15	smooth proper geometrically integral curve `C/k`, following Kleiman, "The
16	Picard scheme", §2 and §4 (cf. FGA Explained Ch. 9; arXiv:math/0504020).
17	
18	The relative Picard functor is
19	
20	```
21	picSharp C := PicSharp.relPresheaf C ⋙ forget AddCommGrpCat
22	```
23	
24	the set-valued shadow of the `H_T`-coset carrier
25	`T ↦ Pic(C ×_k T)/π_T^* Pic(T)` of `Picard/RelPicFunctor.lean` (Kleiman §2
26	Def. `df:Pfs`; blueprint `def:rel_pic_sharp`). A `RepresentableBy` witness
27	against it is a natural bijection
28	`(T ⟶ Pic_{C/k}) ≃ Pic(C ×_k T)/π_T^* Pic(T)`, which is what the downstream
29	tangent-space computation (`AJC.pic0av`, `Pic0.tangentSpaceIso`) attaches to.
30	
31	## The étale-sheafification route (owner decision of 2026-07-28)
32	
33	Kleiman §4 represents the **étale-sheafified** functor `Pic_{(C/k)ét}`, and
34	that is what this file's obligation is stated against —
35	`fgaPicardRepresentability`, over an **arbitrary** base field, with **no
36	hypothesis on `C(k)`**. The functor is built and its sheaf property proved in
37	`Picard/PicEtSheaf.lean` (`PicScheme.picEt`, `picEt_isSheaf_forget`), by
38	sheafifying the relative Picard presheaf for Mathlib's big étale topology
39	localised at `Spec k`.
40	
41	Why the sheafification is not optional. The plain relative functor
42	`picSharp C = T ↦ Pic(C ×_k T)/π_T^* Pic(T)` is not representable over a
43	general field, so an unconditional `RepresentableBy` against `picSharp` is a
44	**false** statement, not merely an unproved one.
45	
46	**CITATION CORRECTED 2026-07-29 (`review-ajc`), by reading the source. The
47	conclusion above is right; the reason previously given for it was not.** This
48	paragraph used to say `picSharp` "is not even a Zariski sheaf (Kleiman §2
49	L1292–L1302)". Those lines
50	(`references/kleiman-picard-src/kleiman-picard.tex`, the full paper) say
51	something else: "The **absolute** Picard functor `Pic_X` is never a separated
52	presheaf in the Zariski topology", proved with the `ℙ¹_X`/`O(1)` argument. That
53	is about `Pic_X`, **not** about the relative `Pic_{X/S} = picSharp`, which is
54	*defined* by quotienting out `Pic(T)` precisely to defeat that argument. What
55	Kleiman actually asserts about the relative functor is weaker (L1330): "Since
56	`Pic_{X/S}` is not *a priori* a sheaf, it is remarkable that it is representable
57	so often in practice." Not-a-priori is not never — indeed L1600–L1605 proves
58	`Pic_{X/S} ≅ Pic_{(X/S)zar}` whenever `f` has a section.
59	
60	**The witness, and it satisfies exactly this file's binders.** Kleiman
61	L5105–L5108 (repeated L5126–L5129): take `X : u² + v² + w² = 0` in `ℙ²_ℝ`, a
62	smooth plane conic — hence smooth, proper, and geometrically integral, since
63	`X_ℂ ≅ ℙ¹_ℂ` — over a field where it has **no** rational point. `Pic_{(X/ℝ)ét}`
64	is representable by §4 `th:main`, the two functors differ (Exercise `ex:Pfs`),
65	and Kleiman concludes `Pic_{X/ℝ}` is not representable.
66	
67	**That last step is now a Lean theorem rather than a quotation**, which is the
68	right state for something this load-bearing:
69	`PicScheme.not_exists_representing_picSharp_of_not_isIso`
70	(`Picard/PicEtSubcanonical.lean`, `ajc-p1`) derives *from* `¬ IsIso

75	`φ^* O(1)` and `h⁰` on `ℙ¹_ℂ`), which is where Kleiman's own argument lives and
76	is not yet formalised.

78	**Do not route this through a Zariski-sheaf claim** (corrected again the same
79	day, after `work-reviewer` refuted the first repair — see `I-0970`). It is
80	tempting to argue "representable ⟹ Zariski sheaf, and `picSharp` is not one";
81	the second half is *not* what the sources say. `ex:Pfs` compares
82	`Pic_{(X/ℝ)zar}` with `Pic_{(X/ℝ)ét}` — both already sheaves — so it witnesses

113	  simply conditional statements until restated against `picEt`.

116	
117	* `fgaPicardRepresentability` — **the project's central open obligation**:
118	  representability of `Pic_{(C/k)ét}` over an arbitrary field, no rational
119	  point. The file's only `sorry`.

121	  `instPicSchemeEtLocallyOfFiniteType`, `instPicSchemeEtIsSeparated`,
122	  `groupSchemeStructureEt` — the unconditional étale interface derived from it.
123	* `picEtComparison_isIso_of_hasRationalPoint`, `picSchemeOfHasRationalPoint` —
